transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
A Thanksgiving nor'easter brought strong winds and heavy rain to much of the East Coast.
Hundreds of thousands of utility customers lost power on Thursday as winds brought down
trees and power lines.
NPR's Catalan Store of Reports' damage assessments are underway in parts of the Northeast.
Flooding really caused most of the damage and disruptions.
In New York City, emergency crews had to rescue people from flooded cars, and in parts of
New Jersey, several bridges were shut down because of the storm.
In the coastal parts of Virginia, streets were flooded so badly that people were seeing
kayaking through busy streets.
A lot of those bridges and road closures should be reopening as the weather clears up throughout
the day.
That's NPR's Catalan Store of Reporting.
On the West Coast, unusually high tides, known as king tides, could bring more coastal flooding
today from California to Washington State.
President Trump's son-in-law and peace envoy, Jared Kushner, says Russian President Vladimir
Putin has "shown restraint in the war against Ukraine by not using nuclear weapons."
Kushner was speaking on a podcast hosted by the CEO of the company that owns Politico.
Dilla Marks reports.
On the MD Meets podcast with Axel Springer Chief Matias Dovna, Kushner called Putin a
grandmaster of politics and credited him with holding himself back.
So far Putin has showed restraint.
He's agreed not to use nuclear weapons, which obviously is a big thing, and he's reassured
us that that's not his intention.
Kushner said he believes Putin wants peace between Russia and Ukraine.
He also said peace talks should focus most of all on ending the war, not deciding which
side is right or wrong.
But there's a little sign the war itself is winding down.
President Vladimir Zelensky said in his nightly address to the nation Thursday that Russia
was preparing a new mass strike in the coming days.
He also urged Ukrainians to pay attention to missile alerts.
For NPR News, I'm Willem Moggs.
The Iraqi government is closing border crossings run by Kurdish government forces.
NPR's Jan Araf reports it's a controversial move to take back control from the Kurdistan
region.
Iraqi state media says border forces have closed a crossing with Syria and another with
Iran in territory administered by the Kurdish regional government.
Kurds broke away from central government control under Saddam Hussein in 1992 and now administer
four majority Kurdish Iraqi provinces, including border operations.
Earlier this week, the Iraqi prime minister announced that the federal oil ministry would
now run some of the biggest oil fields that are currently managed by Iraq's Kurdistan
regional government.
It accuses Kurds of diverting oil proceeds.
They deny it.
The Kurdish leadership says it will not give up control of its borders or the oil fields.
Jan Araf, NPR News, Amman.
This is NPR News in Washington.
The Environmental Protection Agency says test results could come in today from samples collected
following Wednesday's controlled explosion of a stockpile of hazardous chemicals in southeast
Iowa.
The EPA took more than 1,500 samples of air, water, soil and dust before the blast and
more than 1,000 more afterward.
So far, the agency has not reported finding lead in the air since the blast.
The Army says the stockpile of lead azide was deteriorating and could have exploded
on its own as temperatures dropped.
Airbnb is taking a closer look at what guests are required to do before they check out.
The company has started reviewing listings under a new house rules policy that took effect
last week.
NPR's Michaela Gray reports guests have been sharing some of the more demanding checkout
instructions from Airbnb hosts on social media.
Taylor Runfro, a social media travel influencer, has contributed to the online discourse against
strict hosts.
She says she's experienced unreasonable cleaning expectations before the policy change and
has moved toward staying in hotels instead.
You don't have to worry about any of those cleaning things and most of the time you get
a continental breakfast and people come in and clean your room every morning.
So it's like, it is a better deal.
The new policy says house rules should be reasonable.
For example, hosts can ask guests to put used dishes in the sink, but shouldn't ask them
to wash or put them away.
Airbnb says it'll now be looking at listings and emailing hosts if their house rules appear
to be violating the new policy.
Michaela Gray, NPR News This message comes from NPR sponsor Charles
Schwab.
When is the right time to sell a stock?
How do you protect against inflation?
Financial decisions can be tricky and often your own cognitive and emotional biases can
lead you astray.
Financial decoder and original podcast from Charles Schwab can help.
Join host Mark Reapie as he offers practical solutions to help overcome the cognitive and
emotional biases that may affect your investing decisions.
Download the latest episode and subscribe at Schwab.com/financialdecoder.

Jared Kushner says Putin has shown restraint by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine war
Zelensky warns Russia is preparing a new mass missile strike in coming days
Iraqi government closes border crossings run by Kurdish regional government forces
Iraq's federal oil ministry to take over some oil fields managed by Kurdistan region
EPA awaits test results from samples after Iowa controlled explosion of lead azide stockpile
Airbnb begins reviewing listings under new house rules policy limiting checkout demands
